title: Closest pair of points: brute force vs divide and conquer
problem_statement: Given n >= 2 points in the plane with integer coordinates (duplicates allowed), compute the minimum squared Euclidean distance (x_i - x_j)^2 + (y_i - y_j)^2 over all pairs i != j, as an exact integer.

input.size_measure: 2n integer coordinates (bounded by 10^9 in the harness, so arithmetic and comparisons are unit cost).

algorithms.name: all pairs
algorithms.idea: Compute the squared distance of every pair and keep the minimum.
algorithms.pseudocode: best = min over i < j of (x_i - x_j)^2 + (y_i - y_j)^2
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) (exactly n(n-1)/2 distance evaluations on every input)

algorithms.name: Shamos-Hoey divide and conquer
algorithms.idea: Sort by x once; split at the median, solve both halves recursively, and let delta^2 be the better answer. A closer cross pair must lie in the vertical strip of half-width delta around the split; scanning the strip in y order, each point needs comparing only with the next few (at most 7). Each call returns its points sorted by y by merging its halves' lists, so no re-sorting is needed.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n log n) on every input (initial sort plus T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n): linear merge, strip filter and strip scan per level)
algorithms.correctness: Shamos & Hoey 1975; Bentley & Shamos 1976. With xm the x of the right half's leftmost point, every left point has x <= xm and every right point x >= xm, so a cross pair at squared distance < delta^2 has both points within horizontal distance delta of xm. Strip points of one half are pairwise >= delta apart, so a delta x 2delta box holds at most 8 strip points: the inner scan stops after O(1) steps, and it stops early only once dy^2 >= the current best.

shape.note: count depends on the drawn instance; kept so the record says why the diagnostic cannot decide

relationship: Both polynomial: Theta(n^2) -> Theta(n log n). Divide and conquer is optimal in the algebraic computation-tree model, where element uniqueness (and hence closest pair, whose answer is 0 exactly when two points coincide) needs Omega(n log n) (Ben-Or 1983). Allowing randomization and the floor function (grid hashing) gives expected O(n) (Rabin 1976; Khuller & Matias 1995), outside that model.

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree for n = 2..9, 16, 17, 33, 100 and 500 (all pairs capped at n = 500; divide and conquer also at n = 3000) on three instance kinds: generic coordinates in [0, 10^6), a tiny grid of side ~sqrt(n) (duplicate points, answer 0, collinear points), and all points on one vertical line (every point lands in the strip). harness.check is an exact, independent oracle: a plane sweep with pruning along the coordinate of larger spread. V2 (since 2026-10-07, research/2026-10-07b_count_based_v2.md): on points with coordinates in [0, 10^9), the measured quantity is the exact number of MULTIPLICATIONS (a squaring ** 2 counts as one) made by the unchanged implementations, counted by an instrumented integer type (CountingInt in harness.py) that wraps every coordinate; with it both implementations return the same answers as on plain integers (checked at n = 2, 3, 4, 7, 50, 300). All pairs: exactly n(n-1) at n = 125, 250, 500, 1000, 2000 (15500 ... 3998000); alpha = 1.001 against n^2. Divide and conquer, 1 seeded instance per n: 14523, 31335, 68047, 147196, 314573, 674959, 1436363 at n = 1000, 2000, ..., 64000 (1.406 to 1.457 n log2 n), of which the strip filter contributes S(n) = n + S(floor(n/2)) + S(ceil(n/2)) (exactly, e.g. 955392 at n = 64000), the base cases 2 per pair, and the data-dependent strip scan the rest (29% to 31%); alpha = 0.993 against n log n (0.993 to 0.995 over three seeded samples). Comparisons are not counted: those made inside CPython's sorted() and min() differ between Python versions (39380 under Python 3.12.10 vs 39445 under 3.14.2 at n = 1000, experiments/2026-10-07b_count_v2_cross_version.py), whereas the reported multiplication counts are identical under both. Tolerance 0.03: exact counts carry no timing noise, so the band only covers lower-order terms and the data-dependent strip scan (largest |alpha - 1| here 0.007) and stays below half the distance to the nearest rival. Rivals that must NOT fit, all rejected: all pairs against n log n (alpha = 1.721) and n^2 log n (0.926); divide and conquer against n (1.105), n log^2 n (0.902) and n^2 (0.553). The log factor is therefore resolved for both (validator diagnostic, RESEARCH_LOG RL-048). experiments/2026-10-07b_count_v2_closest_pair.py reproduces every count above.

caveats: Squared distances on integer coordinates keep everything exact; with floating-point coordinates the same algorithm works but comparisons are subject to rounding. V2 counts multiplications, not time: 61.5% to 66.5% of the divide-and-conquer count (n = 1000..64000) is the strip filter's one squaring per point per recursion level (n per level over about log2 n levels); the comparisons of the initial sort and of the merges are not counted. The earlier timing fit could not distinguish n log n from n over the measured range (the log factor varies by only ~1.6x); the exact counts do. The Omega(n log n) lower bound holds in the algebraic computation-tree model and does not apply to the randomized grid-hashing algorithms.
notes: The same divide-and-conquer pattern extends to d dimensions in O(n log n) for fixed d (Bentley & Shamos 1976).
